faq.a: Heavy infection causes chronic colitis and mucosal edema, leading to straining and weakening of the rectal wall.
faq.q: Why is Trichuris the main cause in African children?

faq.a: Mild cases may sit, but discomfort and fear of prolapse often cause avoidance of sitting.
faq.q: Can a child with rectal prolapse sit normally?

faq.a: No; most cases respond to deworming, nutrition and stool softening. Surgery is reserved for irreducible or recurrent severe prolapse.

exam: What bedside maneuver distinguishes rectal prolapse from perineal descent? — Ask the child to bear down; a true prolapse shows mucosal tissue protruding, perineal descent shows only soft tissue.

A child from a rural clinic presents with a red mass at the anus and mucus‑stained fingers. Which investigation is most urgent and why? — Stool microscopy for Trichuris eggs; confirming infection directs immediate deworming.
How would you stage a prolapse that reduces easily but the mucosa is edematous? — Stage I (mucosal, reducible) – indicates conservative management.
Why is albendazole preferred over pyrantel for Trichuris in this setting? — Albendazole has proven efficacy against Trichuris and is safe for children; pyrantel is less effective for this species.
A child with rectal prolapse is also severely anemic. What additional treatment is indicated and what must you monitor? — Oral iron supplementation; monitor hemoglobin and gastrointestinal tolerance.
When should you refer for surgical repair? — When the prolapse is irreducible, strangulated, or recurs despite adequate deworming and nutritional support.
What red‑flag symptom would make you suspect strangulation? — Sudden severe pain with a firm, non‑reducible mass and signs of systemic toxicity.
How does malnutrition contribute to rectal prolapse? — It weakens connective tissue and sphincter tone, increasing susceptibility to mucosal protrusion during straining.
ai.title: Rectal Prolapse in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Rectal prolapse is the telescoping of the rectal wall through the anal canal, common in African children with heavy helminth infections. Diagnosis is clinical, staging guides management, and treatment focuses on parasites, nutrition and supportive care.

b: Visible mucosal prolapse on inspection
Blood‑stained mucus on finger during digital exam
Reduction by gentle pressure confirms diagnosis
sections.p: Full-thickness protrusion of the rectal wall through the anal verge, seen as a red, edematous mass that may be reducible.

b: Stage guides urgency of surgical referral
Irreducible prolapse = red flag
sections.p: Use the Oxford (or Goligher) classification adapted for children: Stage I – mucosal only, reducible; Stage II – full‑thickness, reducible; Stage III – irreducible or strangulated.

b: Heavy Trichuris infection → mucosal edema and straining
Severe malnutrition → weakened sphincter and connective tissue
Chronic constipation from low fibre diet
Associated conditions: HIV, sickle cell disease, schistosomiasis (causing portal hypertension)
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the leading cause is chronic Trichuris trichiura infection, followed by malnutrition, constipation and pelvic floor weakness.

b: Mass appears when child bears down
Mucus‑stained finger after digital exam
Pain is usually mild unless strangulated
sections.p: Parents report a reddish mass protruding during or after a bowel movement, often with mucus, occasional bleeding, and difficulty sitting.
Most work‑up is bedside; laboratory tests help identify underlying infection or anemia.

t.b: Detects Trichuris eggs; positive result confirms parasitic cause
Looks for anemia from chronic blood loss or hookworm; low hemoglobin prompts iron therapy
Low albumin suggests severe malnutrition; treat with nutritional rehab
Positive result alters infection prophylaxis and follow‑up

b: Irreducible prolapse – risk of necrosis
Severe bleeding or shock
Fecal incontinence from sphincter damage
sections.p: Complications arise from ischemia, ulceration or strangulation of the prolapsed segment.

b: Iron supplementation for anemia – oral ferrous sulfate, avoid IV iron unless severe
High‑fiber diet, adequate fluids, and stool softeners (e.g., lactulose) to prevent constipation
Manual reduction with gentle pressure; if fails, refer for perineal or abdominal surgery
Avoid steroids unless indicated for another condition; they impair healing
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support nutrition and reduce straining, and intervene surgically only when conservative measures fail or complications develop.

b: Repeat stool exam 2 weeks after treatment
Monthly deworming program in endemic areas
Nutrition counseling – increase fruits, vegetables, legumes
sections.p: Re‑examine after deworming, monitor growth and stool consistency, and educate caregivers on hygiene.

b: Anal fissure – painful tear, no protruding mass
Perineal descent – soft tissue descent without mucosal lining
External hemorrhoids – venous cushions, not full‑thickness rectal wall
sections.p: Conditions that can mimic a protruding perianal mass.

b: Normal stool microscopy does not rule out low‑grade Trichuris infection; repeat if suspicion remains
Absence of visible bleeding does not exclude mucosal ulceration
sections.p: Laboratory or clinical findings that may be falsely reassuring.
